title: Beyond the n log n barrier for unrestricted noncommutative circuits
formal: For every field F, does the minimum size s_F(n) of a fan-in-two noncommutative arithmetic circuit computing Pal_{n,n}(X,Y)=∑_{(i₁,…,iₙ)∈{1,…,n}ⁿ}x_{i₁}⋯x_{iₙ}y_{iₙ}⋯y_{i₁} satisfy s_F(n)=ω(n log n), with no homogeneity or syntactic-degree restriction? Yes: the accepted 2026 result of Raz implies Ω(n^(3/2)), and Shastri’s concurrent preprint states the stronger Ω(n²).
why: Historically isolates the obstruction to stronger lower bounds for unrestricted arithmetic computation when multiplication is noncommutative. The 2026 advances show that the n log n barrier can be crossed without constraining intermediate degrees or preventing reuse of intermediate results.
status_note: Checked 11 September 2026. Raz’s Theorem 1, in the 30 July revision of work accepted at FOCS 2026, gives Ω(n^(3/2)) for the displayed palindrome via variable identification and its full-rank central coefficient matrix. This exceeds n log n and settles the historical threshold. The concurrent stronger quadratic preprint is recorded separately. The theorem, model and parameter match were checked; proofs were not independently audited or formalized.

sentences: The source asks for lower bounds beyond n log n for unrestricted noncommutative arithmetic circuits.
Its palindrome polynomial contains words whose second block reverses the indices of the first.
Earlier improvements imposed restrictions on the syntactic degrees of intermediate computations.
A 2026 result accepted at FOCS gives a sufficient unrestricted lower bound, including for this target after a variable identification.
The historical threshold is therefore resolved; a concurrent preprint states the stronger quadratic bound.

references.title: Lower Bounds for Noncommutative Circuits with Low Syntactic Degree
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 8; PDF page 8

definitions: For each n≥2, X={x₁,…,xₙ} and Y={y₁,…,yₙ} are disjoint alphabets of formal noncommuting variables. A noncommutative polynomial over F is a finite F-linear combination of words in those symbols; multiplication concatenates words and extends bilinearly, so variable order is part of a monomial. Pal_{n,n} has 2n variables, degree 2n and coefficients zero or one. A circuit is a finite acyclic graph whose leaves are variables or arbitrary constants from F and whose internal nodes are binary addition or binary multiplication gates. Multiplication inputs have a designated order. There is one output, fan-out is unrestricted, and the circuit must compute the formal polynomial exactly. Its size is the total number of nodes, as in the original paper. Division gates are not allowed; subtraction is available through the field constant −1. There is no bound on depth, intermediate polynomial degree, coefficient size or circuit uniformity. The syntactic degree of a variable leaf is one and of a constant leaf zero; an addition gate takes the maximum of its children’s syntactic degrees and a multiplication gate takes their sum. The circuit’s syntactic degree is their maximum over all nodes. A polynomial is homogeneous when every nonzero monomial has the same degree; the circuit need not have homogeneous intermediate outputs. The asymptotic claim means: for every fixed field F and every K>0, there is n₀(F,K) such that all n≥n₀ and all circuits computing Pal_{n,n} have more than Kn log₂n nodes. Explicitness is supplied by the displayed polynomial: a word’s coefficient is determined by checking its length, the two alphabets, and the reversed index sequence in time polynomial in n and the word length.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the displayed unrestricted-circuit lower bound beyond every constant multiple of n log n. Bounds only for formulas, homogeneous circuits or restricted syntactic degrees do not suffice. The accepted Raz theorem already proves this claim; a matching quadratic lower bound is stronger than the threshold originally asked for.

context_blocks.title: Multiplication remembers the order of operations
context_blocks.text: The monomials x₁x₂y₂y₁ and x₂x₁y₁y₂ are different formal words. In the palindrome polynomial, a sequence of x-indices is followed by the reversed sequence of y-indices. This supplies a concrete family in place of the original extraction’s phrase such lower bounds.

context_blocks.title: Intermediate computation was the missing freedom
context_blocks.text: A circuit may create high-degree terms that later cancel, even when its final output has modest degree. The earlier results restricted such intermediate behavior. The question was whether the lower-bound barrier could be passed while allowing every circuit in the model.

context_blocks.title: The original gap and the newer result
context_blocks.text: The source records a general Ω(n log n) bound and improves it under syntactic-degree restrictions. Raz’s accepted result gives Ω(n^(3/2)) for an explicit degree-proportional family and also applies to the palindrome target after identifying corresponding x and y variables. No extra restriction on the original circuit is needed.

context_blocks.title: How the theorem matches the palindrome target
context_blocks.text: Identifying yᵢ with xᵢ turns the polynomial into a one-alphabet palindrome of degree 2n. Its matrix of coefficients indexed by length-n prefixes and suffixes is a permutation matrix: a word occurs exactly when the suffix reverses the prefix. The matrix is full rank over every field, so Raz’s Theorem 1 supplies Ω((2n)√n) product gates. Variable identification cannot increase circuit size; hence this also lower-bounds circuits for the original two-alphabet polynomial.

context_blocks.title: A stronger concurrent statement is recorded separately
context_blocks.text: Shastri’s revised May preprint states a tight Ω(nd) bound for Pal_{n,d}, giving Ω(n²) when d=n. The card’s resolved n log n threshold does not depend on independently accepting that stronger proof: the accepted Raz result already crosses the required threshold.
